classification_signals: The paper explicitly states 'The purpose of this study was to see if we could demonstrate a clear relationship between the presence of daylight and human performance in buildings. In this study we used a statistical technique called multivariate regression analysis...' (Page 2). It describes data collection from three school districts, defines variables like 'Window Code', 'Skylight Code', and 'Daylight Code', and presents statistical results (p-values, effect sizes) in tables and text for student test scores (Pages 6-9). The discussion section interprets these findings and addresses limitations of the observational design (Pages 11-15).
title: Daylighting Impacts on Human Performance in School
authors: Lisa Heschong, Roger L. Wright & Stacia Okura, 2002

limitations: The statistical analysis cannot prove causality, only correlation.
The reason for the observed effects is left to hypothesis.
Potential teacher assignment bias (e.g., more skilled teachers preferentially assigned to daylit classrooms) could confound results, though analysis found no significant association.
Curriculum differences between schools within districts were not fully controlled for.
Daylight code is an indicator of potential daylight, not actual illumination levels or conditions over time.
Insufficient funds to sample enough classrooms for comprehensive illumination measurements.
Site visits were only at one point in time, lacking information on how teachers actually operated classrooms (e.g., turning lights on/off, using shades).
The Fort Collins district had the least amount of information about student and school characteristics, potentially influenced by unknown variables.
Poor lighting quality from south-facing monitors in Fort Collins, leading teachers to keep shades down, may have weakened the skylight variable's positive effect.
The small R² for the daylight variable (e.g., 0.003 in Capistrano math model) suggests a small effect size, despite statistical significance.
minimum_safe_summary: This observational field study investigated the impact of daylighting on human performance in elementary schools across three districts in California, Washington, and Colorado. Using multivariate regression analysis on standardized student test scores, the study found a consistent and statistically significant positive association between the presence of daylight (from windows and skylights) and improved student performance in both reading and math. For instance, Capistrano classrooms with the highest window code were associated with 15-23% faster improvement, and Seattle students in daylit classrooms scored 9-15% higher. However, the study acknowledges several limitations, including its associational nature (not proving causality), potential teacher assignment bias, the use of a daylight potential code rather than real-time illumination data, and the inability to fully control for all curriculum or teacher-specific variables.
